origin: Stand-up craft (Chris Head; Geoff Whiting)
variations: Write a bespoke put-down for every line of a transcribed real heckle exchange.

name: Comparison Two-Column Mining
description: Pick two subjects, list every association for each in parallel columns, then mine the overlaps and surprising contrasts for comparison jokes.
instructions: 1) Choose two subjects - one your topic, one to compare it to (can be unrelated). 2) Make two columns. 3) Under each, freely list associated words, traits, clichés, and images - don't force connections yet. 4) Scan for overlapping or clashing keywords between columns. 5) Build jokes asserting the similarity in the setup and exposing a surprising difference (or vice versa) in the punch. 6) Keep the 3 sharpest links.
origin: Comedians on the Loose joke-writing techniques
variations: Force the second subject to be random (open a dictionary, point).

name: Statistic Afterthought One-Liners
description: Use real or absurd statistics as setups, then add an afterthought that takes a surprising attitude or deliberately misreads the number.
instructions: 1) Collect 10 statistics (real headlines or odd survey facts like '8% of people pronounce Wi-Fi wiffy'). 2) For each, state the stat plainly as a setup. 3) Add an afterthought payoff that either (a) takes an unexpected attitude to it, or (b) wilfully misinterprets what the number means. 4) Write at least one per stat; push for 30 across a session to keep ~10. 5) Tighten: cut words, end on the funniest word.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11: Writing Wordplay One-liners
variations: Inspirational-quote version: use a motivational quote as setup, knock it down cynically.

name: Saying Recompletion
description: Begin a well-known saying so the audience predicts the ending, then complete it with a surprising twist - a fast, reliable misdirection one-liner form.
instructions: 1) List 10 sayings, proverbs, or cliches with predictable endings ('Behind every great man...', 'Money can't buy...'). 2) Say each normally up to the point of expectation. 3) Replace the expected ending with a surprising one; the bigger the departure (while still making sense), the bigger the laugh. 4) Write 2-3 endings per saying and keep the best. 5) Read aloud to confirm the misdirection lands on the final word.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11; classic 'afterthought/recompletion' gag form
variations: Saying-reversal version: take the saying literally and build a scenario around the literal meaning.

name: Idiom Beforethought (Wordplay Reverse-Build)
description: Start from a phrase or idiom that has two meanings or a homophone, treat it as the payoff, and build a setup backwards so both meanings fire at once.
instructions: 1) Google an idiom list, or collect homophones/double-meaning phrases ('it hit me', 'Chinese whispers'). 2) Pick one as your intended PAYOFF. 3) Work backwards: invent a literal scenario where the phrase's other meaning is literally true. 4) Write a setup for that scenario - but avoid using the payoff's key word in the setup (or the surprise dies). 5) Land the phrase as the final beat so both meanings collide. 6) Produce several; keep the cleanest.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11: Writing Wordplay One-liners
variations: Pun-payoff version: take any pun and reverse-engineer a clean setup that hides the key word.

name: Hide the Payoff Word
description: Editing drill that strengthens any joke by removing words from the setup that telegraph the punchline, using synonyms, specifics, or roundabout phrasing.
instructions: 1) Take 5 of your existing jokes. 2) Identify the key word(s) in each payoff. 3) Scan the setup: is that word (or an obvious cue to it) present? If so, the surprise is leaking. 4) Rewrite the setup to avoid the word - use a synonym, a specific detail, or a roundabout phrasing (e.g. say '12:59' instead of 'one' if the punch needs 'one'). 5) Read before/after aloud; the concealed version should land harder. 6) Add this as a permanent step in your editing checklist.
origin: Chris Head, Lesson 11; standard one-liner craft
variations: Reverse audit: deliberately leak the word, then fix it, to feel the difference.

name: Question-What-Nobody-Questions Drill
description: Observational drill: pick an everyday ritual everyone accepts and relentlessly ask why it exists, mining the arbitrary or absurd logic underneath for material.
instructions: 1) Each day pick one mundane routine or convention (tipping, the urinal gap, 'how are you' as a greeting). 2) Ask: why does this exist? Who decided this? What if I refused? 3) Write the absurd assumptions baked into it. 4) Phrase your strongest finding as a setup ('Why do we...?') and draft a punch that exposes the absurdity. 5) Keep a running 'why does this exist' list to pull from.
origin: Observational-comedy pedagogy (Seinfeld 'noticing' strategies)
variations: Contradiction-collector version: log 5 gaps between what people say and what they do.

name: It-Was-So-X-That Exaggeration Drill
description: Fixed hyperbole template that forces fresh, specific exaggerations by completing 'It was so [quality] that ___' with the most extreme believable image.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic and the quality you want to amplify (so quiet, so cheap, so boring, so cold). 2) Complete the template: 'It was so [quality] that ___' with a concrete, surprising consequence ('My apartment was so quiet I thought the flies were studying'). 3) Write 5 completions per quality; the early ones are obvious, the later ones funnier. 4) Make the consequence specific and visual, not generic. 5) Keep the best as one-liners or tags.
origin: Standard humor-writing technique (The Write Flourish; comedy-device guides)
variations: Understatement flip: describe something huge with deadpan minimization ('mild inconvenience').

name: Blind Spot Persona Builder
description: Build a stand-up persona by naming a real personal flaw, exaggerating it, and giving your stage self a 'blind spot' - they're oblivious to the very flaw the audience sees clearly.
instructions: 1) List your genuine flaws (ask close friends: am I controlling, negative, awkward, mean, vain?). 2) Pick the truest one. 3) Exaggerate it to an absurd degree. 4) Create the blind spot: on stage you do NOT see this flaw - you present as its opposite (a controlling person who insists they're easygoing). 5) Give the persona an agenda: something false it's trying to convince the audience of, and will fail to. 6) Write 3 jokes where the gap between how you see yourself and how you obviously are is the engine.
origin: Comedians on the Loose (stage-persona method); Steve Kaplan straight/wavy-line theory
variations: Attitude-list version: from a list of positive/negative qualities, friends pick 3 of each that fit you; build the persona from those.

name: Contrary Attitude Rant
description: Pick something authority or society calls bad and spend two minutes committedly arguing it's actually good - surfacing your contrarian comedic point of view.
instructions: 1) List 5 things 'everyone agrees' are bad (skipping the gym, eating alone, ghosting, being late). 2) Pick one. 3) Set 2 minutes. 4) Argue out loud, fully committed, that it's actually GOOD - with specifics and mock-conviction. 5) Record it; mine the most confidently absurd lines. 6) The strongest become opener premises that announce your persona's worldview.
origin: Stand-up persona/POV pedagogy (Stand Up Comedy Clinic; common class drill)
variations: Reverse: argue that a beloved thing (puppies, weddings, summer) is secretly terrible.

name: Song Parody Rewrite
description: Take a well-known song and rewrite its lyrics for comic effect while preserving melody, meter, and stress - training rhythm, economy, and sustained comic premise.
instructions: 1) Pick a song you know cold; rap or lyric-dense pop gives more syllables to work with. 2) Write out the original lyrics. 3) Choose a single comic concept strong enough to last the whole song (the song is about doing laundry; about your commute). 4) Replace lyrics line by line, matching syllable count and keeping word stress on the musical accents - even one extra syllable dulls the joke. 5) Front-load setups so punch words land on strong beats. 6) Sing it aloud to test scansion; fix any lines that trip. 7) Build to a strongest joke at the final chorus.
setup: a known song and its lyrics
origin: Parody-songwriting tradition (Weird Al Yankovic method)
variations: Genre-swap version: perform a serious song in a wildly wrong style; or parody a jingle/anthem.

name: New Choice
description: Improv wit game: a side-coach 'dings' a player mid-scene and they must instantly replace their last line or action with a different one, training rapid alternative generation under pressure.
instructions: 1) Two players improvise a scene; a host watches with a bell (or just yells 'New choice!'). 2) At any moment the host dings; the player who spoke last must immediately replace their last line with a completely different one. 3) The host can ding repeatedly (3-6 times) on the same line, forcing ever more inventive replacements. 4) The scene continues incorporating whatever the final choice was. 5) Conversation-practice version: a friend asks you a question; every time they say 'again', you must answer the same question a different way - keep going past the point of comfort.
setup: 3+ people (or a partner who calls dings)
origin: Short-form improv canon (Whose Line / Theatresports)
variations: Solo writing version: write 10 different punchline responses to one setup; 'new choice' on physical actions too.

name: Alphabet Scene
description: Two players improvise a scene where consecutive lines must begin with consecutive letters of the alphabet, A through Z. A hard constraint that forces commitment to whatever a difficult letter demands.
instructions: 1) Two players take a scene suggestion and a starting letter. 2) Player one's line starts with that letter; player two's reply starts with the next letter; alternate through the alphabet, wrapping after Z. 3) Keep the scene's story real - the letters should serve the scene, not replace it. 4) Hesitating, skipping, or wrong letters = restart or swap players. 5) Target: complete all 26 lines in under 4 minutes. Pair conversation version: chat about your day in alphabetical sentences.
origin: Theatresports / Whose Line short-form game
variations: Solo writing version: write a 26-line monologue, each sentence starting with the next letter.

name: Scenes From a Hat
description: A host draws rapid-fire comedic prompts ('things you shouldn't say at a funeral') and players step forward with instant one-line takes. Maximum reps of premise-to-punchline speed.
instructions: 1) Beforehand, write many funny prompts on slips ('things you can say to your dog but not your boss', 'rejected superhero powers', 'world's worst first-date openers'). 2) Put them in a hat. 3) Draw one and immediately perform or pitch the funniest short response - one line or a 10-second bit, then blackout. 4) Move fast; multiple players can jump in on the same prompt. 5) The discipline is getting to the joke in the first beat. 6) Keep the prompts that generate the most material for later writing.
origin: Whose Line Is It Anyway / short-form improv
variations: Solo version: random prompt generator, say three different takes aloud per prompt in 30 seconds.

name: Three Perceptual Positions Act-Out
description: Greg Dean's funny-storytelling drill: tell a personal story while consciously switching between three positions - Narrator (to the audience), Self-in-scene, and other Characters - to mine humor from acting it out.
instructions: 1) Pick a true story with conflict and strong emotion (an argument, a mishap). 2) Map three positions: NARRATOR (you, talking to the audience, setting up and cracking wise), SELF (you, replayed inside the scene), CHARACTER (others/objects you portray). 3) Run it: narrate the setup, then drop into the scene and act out the back-and-forth as Self and Character, popping back to Narrator to comment. 4) Find the funniest in-scene act-outs (voices, postures, exact dialogue). 5) Record and tighten which lines play best in which position.
origin: Greg Dean, Anatomy of Funny Storytelling
variations: Conversation version: practice telling the same story at dinner, leaning harder into act-outs each time.

name: Gibberish Translation
description: One player 'speaks' an emotional nonsense language while a partner 'translates' it into surprising English; the comedy lives in the gap between tone and translation.
instructions: 1) Pair up: one Speaker, one Translator (get a topic - a speech, a how-to, a confession). 2) Speaker delivers a passionate monologue in pure gibberish - real cadence, big emotion, gestures, NOT monotone. 3) Speaker pauses in chunks; Translator 'translates' each chunk into English that matches the EMOTION but surprises with specifics. 4) Heighten: let the translation reveal increasingly absurd content under the grand delivery. 5) Swap roles. 6) Debrief which translations got the biggest laugh (usually committed delivery + unexpected specifics).
origin: Improv canon (Spolin/Johnstone lineage; ImprovDr, learnimprov)
variations: Solo: deliver a known speech in gibberish on camera, then write the funniest possible 'subtitles'.

name: Comic Throughline Map
description: Vorhaus tool for longer pieces: map a single comic premise across a beginning-middle-end so the same incongruity escalates to a climax instead of jokes wandering.
instructions: 1) State your comic premise as the gap between a comic reality and the real one ('a man who treats his cat like a coworker'). 2) Write the THROUGHLINE: where the premise starts (mild), 3-4 escalation beats where the incongruity intensifies, and the climax (most extreme expression). 3) Audit each beat: does it raise the stakes of the SAME premise, or wander to a new one? Cut wanderers. 4) Add tension-and-release: build pressure, then pop it at each beat. 5) End on the biggest, most inevitable version. 6) Apply to a bit, sketch, or story.
origin: John Vorhaus, The Comic Toolbox (comic throughline; tension and release)
variations: Rule-of-Nine pairing: generate nine premise beats expecting one to survive; map the throughline from the keeper.

name: Tension-and-Release Reps
description: Drill the build-up/pay-off rhythm: deliberately stretch the setup to build anticipation, then release it with the punch, testing different build lengths.
instructions: 1) Take a joke or short story with a clear punch. 2) Write/perform it three ways: minimal build (straight to punch), medium build (one extra tension line), long build (stack 2-3 lines that raise expectation or stakes before the punch). 3) Record all three. 4) Listen for where the release lands hardest - too little build = no payoff, too much = audience drifts. 5) Mark the optimal build length. 6) Practice the 'pop': land the release on the final, funniest word, then stop talking.
origin: John Vorhaus, The Comic Toolbox (tension and release)
variations: Story version: practice withholding the key detail to stretch tension, then release.

name: Character Physicality Walk
description: Build funny characters for act-outs by changing how you walk and hold your body part by part, letting physicality generate personality and voice.
instructions: 1) Stand neutral. 2) Change one physical lead at a time: walk toe-heel, then on inside edges of feet, then outside edges, then lead with the chest, then the chin, then the belly. 3) For each, notice the personality and voice that emerges - say a line in that body. 4) Pick the funniest 2-3 bodies and name them (the chin-leader = the smug boss). 5) Improvise a 30-second monologue in each. 6) Bank these physical characters for act-outs in your bits.
origin: Physical-comedy/acting pedagogy (theatre character-physicality drills)
variations: Animal version: walk as an animal, then humanize it 50% to find a character.

name: Just a Minute
description: Speak for 60 seconds on a surprise topic without hesitation, repetition, or deviation, while opponents buzz in to challenge any slip. A classic BBC radio game that builds fluency and composure under interruption.
instructions: 1) One player is given a random subject and must talk about it for 60 seconds. 2) Three rules: no HESITATION (no pauses or filled 'um'), no REPETITION (don't repeat a significant word/phrase), no DEVIATION (stay on topic and on coherent English). 3) Other players listen and buzz/shout to challenge any infraction. 4) If the challenge is correct, the challenger takes over the topic for the remaining time; if wrong, the speaker keeps going. 5) Whoever is speaking when the minute ends scores a point. Rotate subjects.
setup: topics, a timer, a buzzer or hand-raise
origin: BBC Radio 4 panel game (Ian Messiter, 1967)
variations: Solo: record yourself doing 60-second runs on random nouns; self-flag any hesitation/repetition.

name: Intentional Misinterpretation Drill
description: Practice deliberately 'misunderstanding' a phrase - taking the literal, alternate, or absurd reading - as a fast conversational comedy reflex.
instructions: 1) Collect 15 everyday lines people say ('Can you give me a hand?', 'I'm dying for coffee', 'What's the damage?'). 2) For each, write the deliberately wrong reading - literal, second-meaning, or absurd ('Give you a hand? I'm not a surgeon'). 3) Keep it playful, never hostile. 4) Drill aloud for speed: partner feeds lines, you fire the misread within 2 seconds. 5) In real conversation this week, catch one literal-reading opportunity per day. 6) Note which misreads land vs. confuse.
setup: list of common phrases; optional partner
origin: Conversational-humor/banter pedagogy; classic comedy 'misunderstanding' trope
variations: Malapropism version: deliberately swap a word for a similar-sounding wrong one.

name: Amplify and Agree
description: Comeback drill: instead of denying a tease or insult, agree with it and exaggerate it to an absurd degree, defusing the jab and getting the laugh.
instructions: 1) List 10 common jabs you might get ('you're so short', 'you're always late', 'nice pancakes'). 2) For each, agree and overshoot to absurdity ('Short? I get my clothes from the American Girl doll section'). 3) Drill aloud for speed: partner throws light jabs, you amplify-and-agree within 2 seconds. 4) Keep tone warm and self-amused, not defensive. 5) Bank your best three as all-purpose responses. 6) Field-test: next time someone teases you, try it.
origin: Witty-banter / social-skills pedagogy
variations: Pair 'roast-and-amplify': trade light jabs, each must amplify-and-agree before countering.

name: Affectionate Tease + Compliment Reps
description: Practice gentle teasing of a friend's harmless quirk immediately balanced with a genuine compliment, building playful banter that stays kind.
instructions: 1) Identify a friend's harmless quirk (over-organized, always early, loves a niche show). 2) Write a light tease that pokes the quirk ('You alphabetize your spices?'). 3) Pair it with a sincere compliment ('...honestly I admire that discipline'). 4) Aim for a 2:1 compliment-to-tease ratio overall. 5) Drill: write 10 tease+compliment pairs for people you know. 6) Deliver one per day in real life; note reactions, adjusting warmth.
origin: Conversational-humor pedagogy (banter guides)
variations: Self-tease version: tease your own quirk then reframe it as a strength.

name: Useless Superpower Questions
description: Build and deploy a bank of playful 'twist' questions (e.g. 'what's your most useless superpower?') that reliably spark funny back-and-forth in conversation.
instructions: 1) Write 10 absurd/twist questions: 'What's your most useless superpower?', 'What crime would you be surprisingly good at?', 'What's the worst possible name for a cruise ship?'. 2) For each, prepare your own funny answer first (modeling invites theirs). 3) In conversation, drop one and 'yes-and' their answer - build on it rather than topping it. 4) Track which questions consistently produce laughs and keep them in rotation. 5) Retire questions that fall flat; write fresh ones weekly.
setup: notes app for your question bank
origin: Conversational-humor/banter pedagogy
variations: Group icebreaker: everyone answers the same absurd question, vote funniest.

name: Association Speed List
description: Daily one-minute drill listing everything a random object reminds you of, building the associative speed that underpins fast, witty connections.
instructions: 1) Set a 1-minute timer. 2) Pick a random object in view (a mug, a stapler). 3) Rapid-fire write everything it reminds you of - memories, look-alikes, uses, feelings, related words ('mug = morning, pottery class, mugshot, a punch, hot chocolate'). 4) Don't judge; quantity over quality. 5) Next day, new object. 6) Weekly, scan lists for the surprising associations and turn 2-3 into comparison jokes or banter lines. The reps make connections fire faster live.
origin: Witty-banter / improv association pedagogy
variations: Pair version: partner says a word, you free-associate aloud for 20 seconds without stopping.

name: THREES Checklist Pass
description: Run each draft joke through Helitzer's six humor ingredients - Target, Hostility, Realism, Exaggeration, Emotion, Surprise - and rewrite to strengthen whichever is weakest.
instructions: 1) Take 5 draft jokes. 2) For each, rate presence of all six THREES ingredients: is there a clear TARGET? Can phrasing raise audience HOSTILITY toward it? Is the underlying REALISM/truth visible? Would EXAGGERATION sharpen it? Is there an EMOTION hook in the setup? Is the SURPRISE maximized at the end? 3) Find the missing/weak ingredient and rewrite to add it. 4) Re-rate; the strongest jokes score on all six. 5) Cut jokes that can't be made to hit at least four.
origin: Mel Helitzer & Mark Shatz, Comedy Writing Secrets (THREES formula)
variations: Diagnostic version: take a bombed joke and identify which of the six ingredients was missing.

name: Hostility Target List
description: Helitzer's material-generation drill: list everything you feel genuine hostility toward, vent freely about why, and harvest premises - because hostility plus truth is a reliable laugh engine.
instructions: 1) Free-list people, things, institutions, and situations you feel real hostility or frustration toward - no self-censoring. 2) For each, write why it frustrates you, exaggerating your emotional state to full rant. 3) Don't try to be funny; just vent honestly and specifically. 4) Review: the items with the most heat and specific grievances are your strongest premises. 5) Narrow each hot target to a single sharp premise sentence. 6) Develop the top 3 into bits using your joke-structure drills.
origin: Mel Helitzer & Mark Shatz, Comedy Writing Secrets
variations: Love version: list things you irrationally love and over-defend them.

name: Add Act-Outs with Space Work
description: Judy Carter's drill: convert a told joke into a performed one by turning the people/objects in it into act-outs, then add mimed 'space work' to make the act-out physically real.
instructions: 1) Take a joke where you currently just TELL what happened. 2) Find the moment to act out - become the person or thing in the joke (your boss, your dog, the GPS voice). 3) Replace narration with first-person dialogue in their voice. 4) Add space work: mime the objects and environment (hold the invisible phone, open the invisible fridge) so the scene is physically real. 5) Record; check the act-out lands harder than the told version. 6) Add act-outs and space work to 3 jokes.
setup: video recorder; existing jokes; room to move
origin: Judy Carter, The Comedy Bible (Act-Out, Space Work)
variations: Pair version: a friend calls out which line to act out, you must instantly perform it.

name: Topic + Attitude = Premise Worksheet
description: Carter's premise builder: combine a TOPIC with your ATTITUDE about it to write a sharp premise sentence that cuts to the chase, the springboard for jokes and act-outs.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic you're passionate about. 2) Write your honest ATTITUDE toward it in one phrase (love/hate/confused/scared). 3) Combine into a premise that cuts to the chase - not a description of what happened, but the pointed claim ('Online dating is a job interview where both people lie on the resume'). 4) Test it: does it state a clear opinion AND imply jokes? 5) Generate 3 jokes off the premise, then add an act-out. 6) Repeat for your top 3 topics.
origin: Judy Carter, The Comedy Bible (setup = topic + attitude + premise)
variations: Mind-map version: mind-map your top 3 topics first, then pull premises from the densest branches.

name: Association List + Find the Connector
description: Greg Dean warmup: build a long association list of specific details about a topic, then hunt for words with two interpretations (connectors) to seed misdirection jokes.
instructions: 1) Pick a topic. 2) Ask 'what are all the things I can think of that relate to this?' and list specific, identifiable details - aim for 30+. 3) Scan the list for any word or phrase with two possible interpretations (a connector). 4) For each connector, note the expected interpretation (the target assumption a setup would create) and an alternate one. 5) Write a setup that leans on the expected meaning, then a punch that reveals the alternate (the 2nd story). 6) Mine several connectors from one list.
origin: Greg Dean, Step by Step to Stand-Up Comedy (Joke Map / association list)
variations: Speed version: 1-minute association list, then find one connector in 60 seconds.

name: Premise Deconstruction (Monologue Mining)
description: Improv-derived premise generator: speak truthfully on a one-word prompt for 1-2 minutes, then deconstruct the recording for behaviors, characters, objects, and phrases to mine into joke premises.
instructions: 1) Pick one random word. 2) Record yourself talking honestly about it for 1-2 minutes - real memories and opinions, no jokes. 3) Play it back and flag anything that makes you smile. 4) Deconstruct it across categories: patterns of behavior (recontextualize them), emotions expressed, details to heighten with 'what if', minor characters to transplant into new contexts, objects with wordplay, locations with comic weight, standout phrases. 5) Turn the 5 richest finds into premise sentences. 6) The low pressure surfaces premises you'd never write cold.
origin: Armando / monologue-deconstruction improv (Armando Diaz), adapted solo by English Comedy Frankfurt
variations: Group Armando: one person monologues, the team improvises scenes inspired by details from it.

name: Deadpan Delivery Drill
description: Practice delivering absurd or funny lines with a completely flat affect - neutral face, monotone, no winking - so the comedy comes from the gap between content and delivery.
instructions: 1) Take 5 absurd statements or your own punchlines. 2) Record yourself delivering each with ZERO emotional emphasis: neutral face, even pitch, no smile, no build. 3) Resist 'selling' it - the deadpan wants the audience to almost miss the joke for a beat. 4) Compare to an animated take; note which lines actually get funnier dry. 5) Practice the 'no reaction' hold after the line - don't laugh at your own joke. 6) Field-test one deadpan line per day in conversation.
origin: Dry-humor/deadpan performance pedagogy (Backstage; comedy-delivery guides)
variations: Contrast version: deliver the same line deadpan vs. big-and-animated; keep whichever is funnier.

name: Fortunately / Unfortunately
description: A circle story where lines must alternate beginning 'Fortunately...' and 'Unfortunately...'. Drills instant reframing - finding the upside or downside of anything in one breath.
instructions: 1) Sit in a circle. 2) Player 1 opens with a neutral first sentence ('Jeff woke up late for the wedding'). 3) Player 2 adds a sentence starting 'Fortunately...', Player 3 'Unfortunately...', alternating around the circle. 4) Each turn must reverse and escalate the situation logically but absurdly. 5) Keep the chain coherent; build toward a ridiculous climax. 6) Debrief the funniest reversals - they're often the most specific. 7) Solo writing version: alternate the two words down a page.
origin: Classic improv/storytelling parlour game
variations: Real-life version: take an actual setback and alternate five fortunately/unfortunately spins on it; 'Good news/bad news' newsroom framing.

name: Joke Exquisite Corpse
description: Surrealist parlour game adapted to comedy: players blindly contribute setups and punchlines on folded paper, producing absurd joke mash-ups that spark fresh associations.
instructions: 1) Each player writes a joke SETUP on the top of a slip ('Why did the accountant cross the road?'), folds it to hide it, and passes left. 2) Without seeing the setup, the next player writes a PUNCHLINE under the fold and passes again. 3) After a round, unfold and read the mismatched setup/punch pairs aloud. 4) The accidental juxtapositions are the point - mine the funniest collisions. 5) Variation for material: pass premises and have the next person blindly write a tag. 6) Keep any combination that accidentally works.
origin: Surrealist Exquisite Corpse game adapted to joke writing
variations: Single-word version: build an absurd sentence word-by-word, then find the joke in it.

name: Specific Self-Deprecation Drill
description: Write self-deprecating jokes about your real minor flaws, made so vividly specific and imaginative that they read as confident and funny rather than sad.
instructions: 1) List 10 of your minor, situational foibles or one-off embarrassing moments (not deep insecurities). 2) For each, write a joke that's RIDICULOUSLY specific and imaginative - the specificity is what keeps it from sounding sad ('I'm so bad with names I introduced my own mother as "this lady"'). 3) Punch from a place of baseline confidence - you're choosing to roast yourself, not begging for reassurance. 4) Keep a 'less is more' rule: pick your best 3, not all 10. 5) Test one in a speech opener or conversation; gauge whether it lands warm.
origin: Self-deprecation/public-speaking humor pedagogy
variations: Reframe version: end each self-burn with a defiant flip that turns the flaw into a weird strength.

name: Object Transformation (Props)
description: Take an everyday object (or no object) and rapidly demonstrate it as many different things as possible through committed mime, training fast visual-gag generation.
instructions: 1) Hold a neutral object (a pen, a scarf, a chair) or mime an empty hand. 2) On a 9-second clock, transform it: show it as a sword, a toothbrush, a baby, a fishing rod - each with distinct physical use and an attitude. 3) Commit fully and treat it as the new thing; the humor is in the speed and creativity, not length. 4) Solo: do 20 transformations of one object against the clock and note the funniest. 5) Group 'Props': teams get a weird object and pitch comedic uses as quick blackout gags. 6) Mine the best transformations for visual bits.
origin: Whose Line 'Props' / Canadian Improv Games object-transformation
variations: The Gift: a partner hands you an imaginary object; you instantly define it as something specific and react.

name: Setup-Reveal-Escalation Sketch Build
description: Write a sketch from a single comic idea using a fixed structure - setup, reveal, escalation, pay-off - keeping one game and two clashing points of view.
instructions: 1) Pick ONE comic idea/game (e.g. a prudish clerk refusing to sell an embarrassing item). 2) Define two clashing POVs: one reasonable character, one unreasonable - each convinced they're right. 3) SETUP: establish who/where/what they want in 3-4 lines. 4) REVEAL: land the bizarre element in one clean hit. 5) ESCALATION: repeat and vary the same conflict, upping absurdity each beat - introduce NO new ideas. 6) PAY-OFF: end on a reversal (the reasonable character adopts the unreasonable view) or a false-dawn fail. 7) Read aloud; cut anything off-game; keep it under ~2 pages.
origin: Chris Head, How Comedy Sketches Work
variations: Constraint: write three different reveals for the same setup, then pick the strongest to escalate.

name: Press Conference / Expert Game
description: One player fields rapid questions as a secret expert or identity they don't know, inventing confident, funny answers on the fly while piecing together who they are.
instructions: 1) Send the 'guest' out of earshot. 2) The group decides the guest's secret identity or absurd expertise ('world's leading authority on breadcrumbs'). 3) Bring them back; they hold a press conference. 4) Reporters ask questions that hint at the secret without naming it. 5) The guest must answer every question in character, confidently and comically, even before they've guessed who they are. 6) Funny comes from committed, specific, confident wrong-sounding answers. 7) Game ends when the guest correctly guesses their identity. 8) Rotate.
origin: Improv short-form canon (Press Conference / Expert)
variations: Interrogation version: a 'suspect' must justify an absurd secret crime under questioning.

name: Zip Zap Zop
description: A circle passes 'energy' with sharp claps and the words zip/zap/zop in strict order; mistakes or hesitation eliminate you. Trains alertness, reaction speed, and staying present.
instructions: 1. Stand in a circle. 2. Player A makes eye contact with someone, claps and points to them while saying 'ZIP!' with sharp energy. 3. That person immediately passes to anyone with a clap-point and 'ZAP!'. 4. The next passes with 'ZOP!', and the cycle continues zip-zap-zop. 5. Demand crisp, punchy delivery and clean eye contact; speed up over rounds. 6. Mistakes (wrong word, no energy) are celebrated and the game restarts.
origin: Theatre warmup tradition; ubiquitous in improv and drama classes
variations: Add 'Boing' to bounce a pass back; add extra sound words traveling the circle simultaneously; eliminate players to a final duel.

name: Pass the Clap
description: Circle warmup where two players clap in perfect unison, passing the clap around the circle; trains shared timing, presence, and giving/receiving attention.
instructions: Stand in a circle. Turn to your neighbor, make eye contact, and try to clap at exactly the same moment they do. The neighbor then turns to the next person and repeats, sending the clap around the circle. Aim for perfect unison rather than speed at first, then accelerate. Add rules: a double clap reverses direction; you can clap across the circle to anyone you make eye contact with.
origin: Standard improv/theatre warmup; taught at Hoopla and most schools
variations: Send two claps in opposite directions and watch the collision; 'whoosh/whoa/zap' variants layer in more signals.

name: Big Booty
description: A rhythmic number-calling game where any hesitation or misspoken number knocks you out. Trains staying mentally present and reacting in tempo without freezing.
instructions: 1) Players line up; each takes a number (Big Booty is position 0, then Number One, Number Two...). 2) Everyone stomps/claps a steady beat and chants 'Big Booty, Big Booty, Big Booty, oh yeah'. 3) On the beat, Big Booty calls 'Big Booty number [X]'; player X must instantly respond 'Number [X] number [Y]', passing to another player, all on rhythm. 4) Miss the beat, say your own number, stumble, or break rhythm = you go to the end of the line and everyone shifts up. 5) Speed up over rounds. The skill is reacting instantly when your number is called while keeping the beat.
origin: American improv warmup tradition (widely used at UCB and colleges)
variations: Use names instead of numbers; faster tempo each round; reverse direction call.

name: Bunny Bunny
description: A group keeps a rhythm and chant while passing a 'bunny' (hand gesture + eye contact) around the circle, with neighbors echoing - three patterns running at once. Trains divided attention, rhythm, and reacting without overthinking.
instructions: 1) Circle up and establish a steady group chant/rhythm (e.g. 'ooh-ahh, ooh-ahh'). 2) One player is the 'bunny': they make bunny-ear hands and, on the beat, pass the bunny across the circle by looking at and gesturing to another player, who becomes the bunny. 3) The two neighbors of whoever holds the bunny do their own side gesture/sound ('Ruckitucki') in rhythm. 4) Keep all three layers going; the passing must stay on the beat. 5) Mistakes just rejoin the flow - speed up gradually.
origin: Improv warmup tradition; popularized in US theaters (title of Gilda Radner biography play)
variations: Speed challenge (how fast before it breaks); add a counter-rotating second bunny.

name: Whoosh
description: Imaginary ball of energy passed around the circle with sounds and gestures; trains offers, acceptance, and physical commitment.
instructions: Circle up. Pass a 'whoosh' (sweeping both hands toward your neighbor with the sound 'whoosh'). Add rules one at a time: 'Whoa' (hands up) bounces it back the other way; 'Zap' sends it across the circle; 'Groovalicious' makes everyone dance in place; 'Freak out' makes everyone run to new spots in the circle. Keep energy high; mistakes are celebrated with a group 'ahhh' and play continues.
origin: Theatre/improv warmup tradition
variations: Let the group invent new calls; play silent with gestures only.

name: Mind Meld
description: Two players simultaneously shout random words, then keep shouting new words that bridge the previous two until they say the same word at the same time. Trains lightning-fast association and dropping internal censorship.
instructions: 1) Stand facing a partner. 2) Count '1-2-3' together and each say a random word simultaneously. 3) Pause a beat, then count again and each say a word that connects the two previous words. 4) Repeat: each round you both try to converge on the obvious midpoint of the last two words. 5) When you both say the same word, celebrate ('Mind meld!') and restart. Speed matters more than cleverness - say the first bridge that comes to mind.
origin: Improv warmup tradition; staple at UCB/iO
variations: Group version: whole circle tries to converge, any two players jump in with bridge words (also called Convergence or 1-2-3-Word).

name: Count to 21
description: The group tries to count to 21 with one voice at a time and no order; trains shared focus, patience, and reading the room.
instructions: Group stands in a circle, often with eyes closed or gazes lowered. Anyone may say the next number, but if two people speak at once, the count restarts at 1. No system or order is allowed — players must sense when to speak. Continue until the group reaches 21. Debrief: what did it feel like when the group rushed vs. settled?
origin: Drama-teacher and ensemble-building tradition
variations: Count higher; recite the alphabet; do it walking around the room.

name: Hot Spot
description: One player sings in the circle's center until someone taps in with a song ASSOCIATED with the last one. Trains association speed plus the courage to jump in before you're ready.
instructions: 1) Circle up; one volunteer enters the center and starts singing any song. 2) After a few lines, anyone may tap them out and start a new song triggered by association with the previous (shared word, theme, artist, vibe). 3) The circle supports: sing along, clap, hum instruments. 4) Never leave someone stranded - tapping in fast IS the exercise. 5) Run 5-8 minutes. Singing quality is irrelevant; hesitation is the only failure.
origin: iO/UCB warmup tradition; standard Harold-team warmup
variations: Made-up Hot Spot (all songs improvised); Story Hot Spot (tell associated stories instead of songs); Rant Hot Spot (associated rants).

name: Bippity Bippity Bop
description: Center player tries to catch circle players off-guard with commands requiring instant 3-person poses; trains reaction speed and teamwork.
instructions: One player stands in the center of the circle. They approach anyone and say 'bippity bippity bop' — the target must say 'bop' before the phrase ends or they replace the center. If the center just says 'bop', the target must stay silent. Add poses: center calls 'Elephant!' (target makes a trunk, neighbors make ears) or 'Palm tree', 'Toaster', 'James Bond' — the three players must form the pose before a count of five. Whoever fails becomes the center.
origin: Theatre/camp game tradition adopted by improv
variations: Invent new three-person poses with the group; eliminate to a final three.

name: Samurai
description: Stylized sword-strike circle game with loud 'HA!' shouts; builds energy, eye contact, and full-body vocal commitment.
instructions: Circle up. One player raises an imaginary sword overhead shouting 'HA!', then slashes it down pointing at another player ('HA!'). The two neighbors of the target simultaneously slash sideways toward the target's belly ('HA!') while the target raises the sword overhead, then the target sends it onward. Keep shouts loud and movements crisp. Players who hesitate or mis-fire are eliminated or simply restart.
origin: Theatre warmup tradition (samurai-movie pastiche)
variations: Slow-motion samurai; whisper samurai; elimination rounds.

name: Eight Things
description: Jump in the middle, get an arbitrary category, and rattle off eight examples without stalling while the group counts you along. Trains confident listing past the point where 'good' answers run out.
instructions: 1) Group circles up; one player jumps to the middle. 2) Another player assigns a category - the weirder the better ('eight types of pudding', 'eight excuses for being late to your own wedding'). 3) The middle player names eight items rapid-fire; the group counts each aloud ('One! Two!...') and cheers on completion ('Eight things!'). 4) Items don't have to be correct or real - committed nonsense beats hesitation. 5) Next player jumps in. Solo version: random category generator, name eight aloud against a 20-second timer.
origin: Improv warmup tradition; common at UCB
variations: Solo version: set a timer and list 8 things in self-chosen categories aloud; '5 Things' with elaborate descriptions of each item.

name: Crazy Eights Shakeout
description: Physical shakeout counting down from 8 on each limb; raises energy and drops physical tension before scene work.
instructions: Standing, shake your right hand 8 times counting aloud '1-2-3-4-5-6-7-8!', then left hand 8, right foot 8, left foot 8. Repeat the cycle with counts of 4, then 2, then 1, getting faster and louder, ending with a big group cheer or jump. Encourage full volume — the point is shared abandon.
origin: Theatre/dance warmup tradition
variations: Count in gibberish or in character voices.

name: Word Association Circle
description: Players pass single-word associations around a circle as fast as possible; the foundational free-association drill.
instructions: Circle up. Player 1 says any word to their neighbor ('ocean'); the neighbor instantly says the first word it triggers ('wave') to the next person, and so on around the circle. Coach: no pausing to be clever, no censoring, no pre-planning while waiting. If the pace drags, restart with a new word. Variation 'Word Ball': throw an imaginary ball across the circle with each association so order is unpredictable.
origin: Classic psychology/improv crossover; in every improv curriculum
variations: Solo version aloud while walking; 'association chain' where you must explain the link; opposites-only round.

name: Name Six
description: A player must name six items in a category before an object passes around the circle back to them; trains listing under time pressure.
instructions: Sit or stand in a circle with a ball or shoe. One player in the center closes their eyes while the object passes; when they say 'stop', whoever holds it gets a category from the center player ('six pizza toppings'). The object immediately continues around the circle and the holder must name six items before it returns to them. Fail and you swap into the center. Keep categories everyday and play fast.
origin: Party/camp game adopted as improv warmup
variations: Name 3 for kids; harder abstract categories for advanced groups.

name: Look Up, Look Down
description: Eye-contact elimination game; desensitizes players to direct eye contact and builds ensemble connection.
instructions: Circle up, everyone looking at the floor. Leader calls 'Look up!' and everyone immediately looks at one specific person's face. If that person is looking back at you, you both shout ('Dude!' or scream dramatically) and step out (or swap places). Leader calls 'Look down', then repeats. Play until two remain, or play no-elimination where caught pairs simply swap spots.
origin: Drama-teacher warmup tradition
variations: Caught pairs perform a 30-second two-line scene before rejoining.

name: The Shakes
description: Players develop rhythmic tremors in a body part and 'throw' them across the circle; trains physical commitment and giving/receiving offers.
instructions: Circle up. One player starts a rhythmic shake in one body part (a hand, a knee, the head), letting it grow. Making eye contact, they 'throw' the shakes to someone across the circle, who 'catches' it in the same body part, lets it migrate somewhere new, then throws it on. Coach full commitment — the shake should look involuntary and be fun to watch.
origin: Drama warmup tradition
variations: Add sound to each shake; shakes intensify each pass until full-body.

name: Danish Clapping
description: Partner clapping-and-gesture mirror game; trains rhythm, peripheral awareness, and celebrating mistakes.
instructions: Face a partner. On a shared rhythm: (1) both slap thighs, (2) each throws both arms up, left, or right, (3) clap. If your arm gestures happen to match, give a high ten and shout 'Hey!' then find a new partner (or keep score). Keep the three-beat rhythm steady; matches are luck, so the game teaches you to enjoy outcomes you don't control.
origin: Scandinavian children's game adopted by improv (taught at Hoopla)
variations: Speed up each round; tournament style with cheering crowds.

name: Creatures of the Deep
description: A physical 'telephone' game where an impression of a sea creature mutates as it passes around the circle; trains copying, exaggeration, and acceptance.
instructions: Circle up. The leader turns to their neighbor and performs a brief full-body sea creature impression with sound. The neighbor copies it as exactly as they can to the next person, and so on around the circle, letting the impression naturally drift and mutate. Start several creatures going at once for chaos. Debrief: copying IS creating — drift happens by itself.
origin: Hoopla Impro beginners curriculum
variations: Any animal category; emotions instead of creatures.

name: Volcano
description: On a called word, the whole group has five seconds to physically build that object together; trains instant wordless collaboration.
instructions: Players mill around the room. The leader calls an object ('Volcano!', 'Microwave!', 'Eiffel Tower!') and counts down from five. Before zero, the entire group must arrange their bodies into one collective version of the object — no talking or negotiating allowed. Hold it, appreciate it, then resume walking. Repeat with escalating absurdity.
origin: Hoopla Impro / general ensemble training
variations: Small teams compete to form the object; add sound effects.

name: Meet and Greet Walkabout
description: Players walk the room greeting each other under changing relational frames (best friends, rivals, exes); trains instant relationship endowment.
instructions: Everyone walks the room. The leader calls a frame: 'Greet each other as long-lost best friends!' Players greet whoever they meet in that frame for ~30 seconds. New frames: suspicious neighbors, superheroes meeting fans, ex-partners, proud parents, spies exchanging codes. Coach players to notice how body, voice, and eye contact change with each relationship.
origin: Hoopla Impro beginners curriculum; common drama warmup
variations: Greet in gibberish; greet at status 1-10.

name: Yipee
description: Players run around jumping and shouting 'YIPEE!' together; a pure joy-and-silliness icebreaker that lowers stakes for everything after.
instructions: Everyone moves around the room. When you approach another player, make eye contact, and jump in the air together shouting 'YIPEE!'. Advanced rule: both players must either jump or stay grounded together — sense it, don't signal it. Final stage: the whole group converges into one synchronized jumping mass.
origin: Hoopla Impro beginners curriculum
variations: Replace YIPEE with character catchphrases.

name: Wild West
description: Circle game passing 'YE-HAH!' with cowboy gestures plus call-outs that change the pattern; trains energy, listening, and rule agility.
instructions: Circle up. Pass 'YE-HAH!' around the circle with a big arm-swing in your best western accent. Add calls anyone can use: 'HIGH-BARN!' reverses direction; 'BANDITS!' means everyone runs to a new spot in the circle. Invent more calls with the group as you go ('SALOON!' everyone mimes drinking). Keep volume and commitment maximal.
origin: Hoopla Impro beginners curriculum
variations: Re-theme to any genre (pirates, soap opera, sci-fi).

name: Anyone Who
description: Circle chair-swap game driven by self-disclosure prompts; doubles as icebreaker and vulnerability practice.
instructions: Sit in a circle of chairs with one fewer chair than players; one player stands in the middle and says 'Anyone who...' plus something true about themselves ('...has a brother', '...has cried at an ad'). Everyone for whom it's true must dash to a new chair (not adjacent); the middle player grabs a seat, leaving a new caller. Encourage prompts that escalate from trivial to genuinely revealing.
origin: Camp/teambuilding game used across improv classes
variations: 'Big Wind Blows' phrasing; truths must be things you've never told the group.

name: Mr. Hit
description: A slow 'zombie' stalks players who must save themselves by calling another player's name; trains name recall and calm under approach.
instructions: Circle up; learn everyone's names first. One player walks zombie-like toward any other player. The target must call out another player's name before being touched — the named player becomes the zombie's new target's savior chain continues. If touched before naming someone, you become the zombie. Speed and panic increase as the game continues.
origin: Drama-teacher warmup tradition
variations: Two zombies at once; zombie moves at normal speed for advanced groups.

name: Yes, And
description: The foundational agreement drill: partners build an idea by accepting each statement and adding new information.
instructions: Pairs. Player A makes a simple statement ('We're painting the fence today'). Player B responds starting literally with 'Yes, and...' — accepting A's reality and adding one new piece of information. Continue alternating, every line starting 'Yes, and', until the idea reaches a natural peak (plan a holiday, design a restaurant, plot a heist). Debrief on the moments someone secretly said no (blocking) or added nothing (hedging). Then replay the same conversation with 'Yes, but' and 'No' rounds to feel the difference.
origin: Core improv principle; codified by Spolin/Johnstone lineages, taught everywhere
variations: 'Yes, because' for justification practice; group planning version ('Let's throw a party!'); physical yes-and where offers are mimed not spoken.

name: Yes, Let's!
description: Group acceptance game: any player proposes an activity and the whole group enthusiastically does it; trains embodied agreement.
instructions: Group mills about. Any player calls out 'Let's all... [ride horses / be librarians shushing / swim through jello]!' Everyone responds 'YES, LET'S!' and commits fully to the activity until someone calls a new one. No vetoes, no half-hearted miming. Coach the group to notice how fast enthusiasm makes even weak ideas fun. Variation 'or Rather Not': players may decline with 'No, let's not' to practice graceful rejection — then return to pure yes.
origin: Viola Spolin / theatre games tradition
variations: Themed rounds (all activities at the beach); silent version with gesture invitations.

name: Word at a Time Story
description: A group tells a single coherent story contributing one word per person around the circle. Trains instant acceptance of offers and trusting the obvious next word at speed.
instructions: Two players (or a circle) tell a story one word per person: 'Once' / 'upon' / 'a' / 'time' / 'there'... Keep grammar intact and the pace conversational. Coach: don't plan your next word; serve the sentence, not your idea. End sentences confidently rather than spiraling. Circle version: go around 10+ players. Pair version: aim for a complete tiny story with a beginning, middle, and end. If stuck, shout 'Again!' and restart with momentum.
origin: Keith Johnstone tradition (Impro for Storytellers); universal curriculum item
variations: Word-at-a-time letter ('Dear Sir...'); word-at-a-time proverb (Wise Wise Wise); two-headed expert answering interview questions one word each.

name: Story Swap
description: One player tells a story until a signal, then the partner continues from the exact word; trains deep listening and seamless co-creation.
instructions: Pairs, plus a director (or timer). Player A starts telling an improvised story. When the director claps and calls 'Swap!', Player B continues instantly from the precise point — mid-sentence, mid-word — matching tone and content. Swap every 10-30 seconds. The story should sound like one teller. Coach against planning ahead and against resetting the story at each swap.
origin: Hoopla Impro curriculum; conducted-story family
variations: Solo practice: swap between two character narrator voices yourself on a timer.

name: Yeah Yeah Yeah
description: Partners co-tell a shared 'memory', enthusiastically taking the story from each other with 'Yeah yeah yeah!'; trains enthusiastic agreement and shared ownership of ideas.
instructions: Pairs. Player A starts 'Do you remember that time we...' and begins a fictional shared memory. Player B interrupts with an enthusiastic 'Yeah yeah yeah!' (big body language) and continues the memory as their own, adding detail. Keep stealing the story back and forth every few sentences with full enthusiasm. The story belongs to both of you; treat every addition as exactly what happened.
origin: Hoopla Impro curriculum
variations: Do it as exaggerating fishermen; as a couple telling their 'how we met' story.

name: Three Sentence Story
description: Players tell a complete story — beginning, middle, end — in exactly three sentences; trains economy and narrative shape.
instructions: In a circle, give each player a title ('The Jealous Lighthouse Keeper'). They must tell a complete story in exactly three sentences: sentence 1 establishes a character and routine, sentence 2 breaks the routine, sentence 3 resolves it. No run-on cheating. Go around several times, increasing speed. Debrief on what makes a story feel complete with so little.
origin: Improv/storytelling pedagogy
variations: One-sentence stories; six-episode version expanding each sentence into a scene.

name: One Minute Life Story
description: Partners tell their real life story in 60 seconds while the other practices pure listening, then recalls it back.
instructions: Pairs. Player A tells their actual life story in one minute; B listens with full attention — no interrupting, minimal nodding, no rehearsing a response. B then repeats back as much as they can ('You were born in..., then...'). Swap. Debrief: what did being truly heard feel like? What did you miss while 'listening'? Used to open courses because it builds trust fast.
origin: Hoopla Impro beginners curriculum; counseling-skills crossover
variations: Story of your name; story of one scar; 30-second re-tell where B tells A's story in first person.

name: Wise Wise Wise
description: The circle invents 'ancient proverbs' one word at a time, sealing each with a group bow; trains collective sentence-building and confident nonsense.
instructions: Circle up. Build a proverb one word per player: 'A' / 'wet' / 'dog' / 'never' / 'doubts' / 'the' / 'moon'. When a sentence lands with proverb-like finality, the whole group intones 'Wise, wise, wise...' and bows. Coach: short words keep it alive; aim for the sentence to END (players love extending forever). Nonsense delivered with gravity is the comedy engine.
origin: Hoopla Impro / word-at-a-time family
variations: Fortune cookie fortunes; horoscopes; advice column answers.

name: I Am a Tree
description: One player strikes a pose declaring what they are; others join the picture one at a time with complementary offers; trains supporting ideas over inventing new ones.
instructions: Circle around an open space. Player 1 steps in, poses, and declares 'I am a tree.' Player 2 joins with something that complements ('I am an apple hanging from the tree'), then Player 3 ('I am the worm in the apple'). Classic version: the starter chooses one element to stay ('The worm stays'), others clear, and the worm restarts a new picture. Speed version (Martha Game): build pictures of 5-8 people as fast as possible with zero thinking. Coach: add to THIS picture, don't import your own idea.
origin: Theatre games tradition; in nearly every curriculum
variations: Add a line of dialogue from each element; pictures must be locations and two players start a scene in them.

name: Machine
description: Players build a machine one body-part-and-sound at a time; the classic physical 'yes and' and group-mind builder.
instructions: One player starts a repeating mechanical motion with a sound. One at a time, others attach themselves with a complementary repeating motion and sound until the whole group is one machine. Leader can adjust speed ('the machine overheats... slows to a stop'). Themed version: build a 'procrastination machine' or 'love machine' where parts express the theme. Debrief how each person's offer changed the whole.
origin: Viola Spolin (Part of a Whole); Boal's Machine of Rhythms variant
variations: Machine of Rhythms (Boal): build from a rhythm not an object; emotion machines; machine that one player must operate.

name: The Because Game
description: Players extend ideas using 'because', distinguishing offers that deepen a scene (vertical) from ones that merely change topic (horizontal).
instructions: Pairs. A makes a statement ('The bakery is closed today'). B responds 'That's because...' and adds a reason that deepens the situation ('...the baker is testifying in court'). A continues 'And because of that...'. Build a chain of consequence 6-10 links long. Then contrast: replay where each response merely adds an unrelated detail, and feel how the scene goes sideways instead of forward. Use in scenes afterward: every third line must be a 'because' line.
origin: Modern improv pedagogy (Reflex Improv and others)
variations: Solo: respond to podcast/radio lines aloud with 'Yes, and that's because...'.

name: That's Right, Bob
description: Two hosts sell a product, each line beginning 'That's right, Bob!'; trains agreement, enthusiasm, and building on a partner's last idea.
instructions: Pairs play TV shopping hosts selling a suggested product (e.g., a self-stirring mug). Every line must start by enthusiastically validating the partner ('That's right, Bob! And it also...') before adding a new feature, story, or price drop. Keep energy at infomercial pitch. The validation phrase forces genuine listening — you can't 'that's right' something you didn't hear.
origin: Short-form/corporate improv training staple
variations: Sports commentators; cooking-show hosts; award-show presenters.

name: Presents
description: Johnstone exercise: one player mimes giving an unnamed gift; the receiver defines it with delight; trains making your partner's offers valuable.
instructions: Pairs. A mimes handing B a present (just a shaped box — A does NOT decide what's inside). B opens it and declares what it is with genuine delight ('A ukulele! You remembered!'), then justifies why it's perfect. Swap and repeat rapidly, 10+ gifts. Advanced: receiver lets the size/weight of the mime inform the gift. Coach: the giver gives 'nothing'; the receiver makes it a treasure — this is how offers work in scenes.
origin: Keith Johnstone, Impro
variations: Giver names the present and receiver justifies loving it; gifts exchanged in character.

name: It's Tuesday (Overaccepting)
description: One player delivers a mundane line; the partner reacts as if it changes their life; trains treating small offers as important.
instructions: Pairs. A says the most boring line possible ('It's Tuesday', 'The mail came'). B 'overaccepts': reacts with a level-10 emotional response and a monologue justifying why this changes everything ('Tuesday?! Then the inspection is TODAY — I never filed the permits...'). Swap. Coach: the reaction must be specific and justified, not random screaming. Then play scenes where every mundane offer gets treated as significant.
origin: Keith Johnstone (overaccepting); drilled at most schools
variations: Dial reactions 1-10 on command; both players overaccept alternately.

name: The Ad Game
description: A team plays an over-enthusiastic ad agency that must instantly agree on a product name, slogan, celebrity endorser, ad concept, and jingle. Trains high-commitment acceptance and building fast on the first idea.
instructions: 1) Get a product (real or absurd: 'self-stirring soup', 'emotional support brick'). 2) The 'agency' brainstorms aloud and must AGREE on, in sequence: a product name, a tagline, a celebrity spokesperson, the content of a TV spot, and finally a sung jingle - everyone shouting 'YES!' to whatever is offered. 3) No idea is rejected; the first offer is the answer. 4) Cap each decision at ~20 seconds. 5) Perform the jingle together to finish.
origin: Second City / corporate improv staple
variations: Impossible-product version (Ad Campaign); solo version writing a full campaign for a random object in 3 minutes.

name: Questions Only
description: Hold a conversation where every line must be a question; answer a question with anything else and you're out. Trains reframing on the fly under a hard constraint.
instructions: 1) Two players start a conversation on a scenario; every utterance must be a question. 2) No repeating the question you were just asked, no rhetorical stalls, no long hesitation. 3) Violators are replaced by the next player in line (line-up elimination format). 4) Advanced rule: each question must start with a different question word (Why/How/When/Where/Who) than the previous one. 5) Play to a winner or just rotate for 10 minutes.
origin: Short-form canon (Whose Line, ComedySportz)
variations: Questions-only argument; 'no questions allowed' inverse scene for contrast.

name: Last Letter, First Letter
description: Each line of dialogue must begin with the last letter of the partner's previous line; trains listening to the very end of sentences.
instructions: Pairs scene with any suggestion. If A's line ends in '...we should escapE', B's line must start with E ('Every door is locked, though'). Keep scene logic alive — the constraint must not kill the relationship or stakes. Buzz and swap on errors, or just self-correct and continue in practice mode. This forces full listening because you cannot plan your line before their sentence ends.
origin: Short-form canon
variations: Alphabet Game (lines start A, B, C... through Z); solo: alternate two characters yourself.

description: Joke-format drill: '185 [suggestion]s walk into a bar...' players improvise puns on the spot; trains joke structure and pun fluency.
instructions: Get a noun suggestion ('185 pencils'). Players step forward one at a time delivering the fixed format: '185 pencils walk into a bar. The bartender says: we don't serve pencils here. The pencils say: [punchline/pun]'. Groans count as wins. Keep volume and confidence even on weak puns — the reps are the point. Run 10-15 jokes per suggestion before switching.
origin: ComedySportz/short-form canon
variations: Solo daily reps with random nouns; alternative formats ('Knock knock' chains).

name: Five Things
description: Name five items fitting a prompt without pausing while the group counts along - a tighter, faster cousin of Eight Things often using location or situational prompts.
instructions: 1) In a circle, a player receives a prompt like 'five things in a wizard's refrigerator' or 'five things you'd find at the bottom of a lake'. 2) They name five without pausing; the group counts each answer aloud and chants 'Five things!' at the end. 3) Pass to the next player with a new prompt. 4) Coach players to answer instantly even with absurd answers - the drill is anti-perfectionism.
origin: UCB/college improv warmup canon
variations: Each answer must be a full sentence; alphabetical answers for advanced rounds.

name: Three-Line Scenes
description: Rapid-fire two-person scenes capped at exactly three lines that must establish who, where, and what; the core scene-initiation drill.
instructions: Two lines of players. The front pair plays exactly three lines: A initiates (establishing something concrete), B responds (adding relationship/context), A responds once more (sealing who/where/what). Then 'scene!' and the next pair goes. Coach: name your partner, state the relationship or activity directly, no questions as initiations. Run 20+ scenes so everyone initiates many times. Debrief which initiations gave the most information.
origin: iO/UCB training canon
variations: Pair drill back and forth; three-line scenes that must start mid-action; emotion-first initiations.

name: Who What Where
description: Scene drill focused purely on quickly establishing character, relationship, objective, and location in the opening moments.
instructions: Two players, 30-60 seconds: start a scene and establish a clear WHERE and WHO (then in later rounds add WHAT objective) as fast and naturally as possible — through behavior and dialogue, not announcement ('Hand me the wrench' + lying under a car beats 'Here we are in the garage'). Coach ends the scene the moment all elements are clear and asks observers to name them. Rotate quickly through many pairs.
origin: Canadian Improv Games five elements; Spolin Where games
variations: Silent round: establish where/who with zero dialogue; audience guesses.

name: First Line, Last Line
description: A scene must begin with one given line and end with another; trains narrative steering toward a destination without forcing it.
instructions: Collect two unrelated lines of dialogue (from the group or slips of paper). Two players begin a scene with line one and must organically arrive at line two as the final line. Coach: don't rush to the last line — build a real scene whose logic earns it. Debrief: when did the steering show? Run multiple pairs with the same two lines to see different routes.
origin: Short-form/drama class canon
variations: Audience-written lines drawn blind from a hat (Blind Line Offers) injected mid-scene.

name: Blind Line Offers
description: Players must instantly justify random pre-written lines pulled mid-scene; the classic justification-under-chaos drill.
instructions: Before the scene, collect 10+ lines of dialogue written by the group on slips ('That's not my llama', 'I never learned to read'). Two players scene normally, but at any point the director points at a player, who draws a slip, reads it as their line, and the scene must justify it completely. Coach: react to the line as if your character meant it; the justification is the partner's job too.
origin: Short-form canon (Whose Line 'Scenes from a Hat' family)
variations: Phone-autocorrect version using random book sentences; solo version justifying random lines aloud.

name: Emotional Quadrants
description: The stage is divided into four zones, each assigned an emotion; players' characters snap to the zone's emotion as they move; trains instant emotional shifts with justification.
instructions: Mark four stage quadrants and assign each an emotion (rage, infatuation, terror, joy). Two players scene with any suggestion; whenever a player steps into a quadrant they must play that emotion fully AND justify the shift within the scene's reality. Encourage deliberate crossing to practice shifts. Coach: emotion changes how you feel about the SAME situation — don't change the topic.
setup: floor divided into four zones (tape optional)
origin: Drama/improv class canon
variations: Audience assigns emotions; zones change mid-scene; volume quadrants instead of emotions.

name: Emotional Rollercoaster
description: A director calls out emotions during a scene and players must instantly switch while justifying the change; trains emotional flexibility on demand.
instructions: Two players scene from a location suggestion. A side-coach calls emotions every 20-40 seconds ('jealousy!... relief!... disgust!'). Players shift their character's emotional state immediately and justify it inside the scene ('...actually, now that I see the receipt, I'm relieved'). Coach for specificity: resentful not just angry; wistful not just sad. End with a debrief on which emotions felt inaccessible — those are homework.
origin: Improv class canon; Whose Line family
variations: Emotion Replay: play the same 1-minute scene three times in three emotions; sliding-scale rounds (anger level 1 → 10).

name: Boring Line, Emotional Dial
description: Deliver an identical mundane line at many different emotions and intensities; isolates subtext and delivery from content.
instructions: Pick one neutral line ('The bus leaves at noon'). Solo or in pairs, deliver it: loud-angry, quiet-angry (death glare), sobbing, suppressing tears, flirtatious, terrified, triumphant. Then run an intensity ladder on one emotion: level 1 (a flicker) to level 10 (full eruption), finding the distinct levels 3, 5, 7. Partner version: B responds with their own neutral line in a complementary emotion, creating an instant scene. Debrief: meaning lived entirely in delivery.
origin: Acting pedagogy adopted by improv (Theatrefolk and others)
variations: Record yourself solo and review; do it with a single word ('Okay') instead of a sentence.

name: Space Jump
description: Nested scenes: players freeze and new players join, starting fresh scenes from the frozen poses, then unwind back through every scene; trains justification and scene memory.
instructions: Player 1 starts a solo scene. Director calls 'Space jump!'; Player 1 freezes and Player 2 enters, starting a brand-new two-person scene justified by the frozen pose. Continue adding players (3-person, 4-person, 5-person scenes). Then unwind: 'Space jump!' removes the last-added player, and the remaining players must resume the PREVIOUS scene exactly where it left off, until Player 1 finishes their solo scene. Coach: re-enter old scenes with their established reality intact.
origin: Short-form canon; Freeze Tag extension
variations: Genre per layer; emotion per layer.

name: Freeze Tag
description: Players call 'Freeze!', take over a frozen player's exact body position, and justify it into a completely new scene; the most famous justification drill in improv.
instructions: Two players start a scene with big physicality. Anyone watching may call 'Freeze!', tap one player out, assume their exact pose, and start a totally different scene justified by the two positions. Keep scenes short (30-60s) and physical so poses stay interesting. Coach: the new scene should come FROM the pose, not a pre-planned idea; call freeze on movement, not on punchlines. Blind Freeze variant: callers stand facing away, then turn and must justify whatever they see.
origin: Theatre games tradition; in every improv curriculum
variations: Blind Freeze (no pre-planning possible); Chain Freeze where each new scene must connect thematically.

name: What Are You Doing?
description: One player mimes an action; asked 'What are you doing?', they must name a DIFFERENT action, which the asker must then mime - a perpetual mismatch loop that splits attention and forces fast invention.
instructions: 1) Player A mimes an activity (brushing teeth). 2) Player B asks 'What are you doing?'. 3) A must answer with anything OTHER than what they're miming ('Walking my crocodile'). 4) B must immediately start miming walking a crocodile. 5) A asks B 'What are you doing?', B names something new while still miming, and so on. 6) Hesitation or naming the actual mimed action means you're out/swap. Speed up over rounds.
origin: Drama games tradition; everywhere from camps to ComedySportz
variations: Initials version (answers must use letters from suggestion); themed categories; whole-circle elimination.

name: Party Quirks
description: A host must guess the bizarre secret identities/quirks of arriving party guests; trains character commitment and indirect communication.
instructions: One host leaves the room; three guests each get a secret quirk/identity (a time traveler who's always 10 seconds in the future; a person convinced they're made of glass). Guests arrive one at a time and mingle, playing the quirk fully without stating it. The host plays the party while trying to guess each quirk; correct guesses send that guest home. Coach guests to escalate clues from subtle to broad, and the host to play the scene, not an interrogation.
origin: Whose Line / short-form canon
variations: Job interview version (interviewer guesses applicants' quirks); Press Conference (one player guesses who THEY are from reporters' questions).

name: Press Conference
description: Answer journalists' questions as a famous figure - without knowing who you are - deducing your identity from the questions while never breaking stride. Trains confident answering amid total uncertainty.
instructions: 1) One player leaves the room; the group picks who they are (historical figure, celebrity) and optionally what they've just done. 2) The player returns and holds a press conference; the others ask leading questions as journalists ('How did the moon's low gravity affect your golf swing?'). 3) The speaker must answer every question fluently IN CHARACTER while privately deducing their identity. 4) Game ends when they work it out and reveal it naturally in an answer. 5) Rotate.
origin: Short-form canon
variations: Mystery product launch (you don't know what you invented); Q&A where the audience knows your scandal but you don't.

name: Hitchhiker
description: Car passengers progressively adopt each new hitchhiker's character trait; trains observation, imitation, and full-cast character infection.
instructions: Four chairs arranged like a car; three players drive and chat. A hitchhiker with a strong character choice (physical + vocal) is picked up; within a minute, ALL passengers gradually catch the hitchhiker's trait. Once everyone is fully infected, the driver exits, everyone shifts one seat, and a new hitchhiker arrives. Coach: catch the trait organically (justify why you're starting to giggle/whisper/preach), not instantly.
origin: Drama/improv games tradition
variations: Emotion hitchhikers; status hitchhikers.

name: Sit, Stand, Lie
description: Three players scene while at all times exactly one must sit, one stand, one lie down; trains stage picture awareness and physical give-and-take.
instructions: Three players, any scene suggestion. The rule: at every moment one player sits, one stands, one lies down — when anyone changes position, the others must instantly rebalance, justifying their moves inside the scene. Coach: justify the WHY ('I'll just rest here while you two argue'); keep the scene's story primary. Audience calls out violations in practice.
origin: Theatre/improv canon
variations: Levels only (high/medium/low); four players with four postures.

name: Give and Take Focus
description: Spolin focus exercise: players practice deliberately taking and giving stage focus through movement, stillness, and voice.
instructions: Group walks the space neutrally. On 'TAKE', one player (self-selected, only one at a time) does something to seize focus — movement, sound, level change — while everyone else actively gives focus (stillness, orientation toward them). On 'GIVE', the focus-holder passes it deliberately to someone else, who must take it. Then run scenes where the director calls 'give'/'take' to make focus-shifting conscious. Debrief: how do you take focus politely in conversation? How do you give it generously?
origin: Viola Spolin, Improvisation for the Theater
variations: No-caller version where the group self-organizes one-focus-at-a-time.

name: He Said, She Said
description: Players alternate narrating stage directions for their partner who must perform them, then speaking their own lines; trains control-sharing and physical offers.
instructions: Two players. A speaks a line of dialogue, then narrates a stage direction for B ('...she said, slamming the oven door'). B must perform the direction, then speak their own line and narrate a direction for A. Continue. Directions must be performable and in the scene's reality. Coach: give directions that make your partner look interesting; perform received directions fully before speaking.
origin: Keith Johnstone tradition
variations: Directions only round (no dialogue); emotional stage directions.

name: Slide Show
description: A presenter narrates a slideshow whose 'slides' are frozen tableaux formed by teammates; trains narration, justification, and tableau work.
instructions: One or two presenters narrate a slideshow about a suggested trip/event. For each 'click', 2-4 teammates instantly freeze into an unplanned tableau; the presenter must justify whatever they see as the next slide ('Here's the moment Greg discovered the bees'). Run 8-12 slides with escalating narrative. Coach posers: make bold, varied shapes; coach presenters: describe what IS there, then add story.
origin: Short-form canon
variations: Expert lecture with diagram tableaux; family photo album.

name: Sound Effects Scene
description: Two players act a scene while two others provide all sound effects vocally; trains offer-reading and audio-physical coordination.
instructions: Two actors take a scene suggestion; two offstage players make every sound effect with their voices (doors, animals, machines). Actors must incorporate and justify every sound, including mistakes; foley players must watch closely and serve the action. Swap roles. Coach: sounds are offers — a surprise dog bark changes the scene; accept it.
origin: Whose Line / short-form canon
variations: Audience members provide sounds; one actor + one foley solo version.

name: Dubbed Movie
description: Two players act in gibberish 'foreign language' while two others dub their voices in English; trains gibberish expressiveness and tight observation.
instructions: Two onstage actors play a scene speaking only gibberish with big physicality and emotional clarity; two offstage dubbers provide synchronized English 'translation' voices. Actors and dubbers co-create: actors leave clear emotional/physical offers; dubbers justify mouth-movement length. Swap roles. Coach gibberish speakers: vary sounds and intonation so the dub has something to ride.
origin: Short-form canon
variations: Poet Translator (gibberish poem + grandiose translation); Interpreter interview for pairs.

name: Gibberish Translator
description: Spolin classic: one player speaks pure gibberish; a translator renders it into English; trains communication beyond words and confident interpretation.
